expectedText:
MUTUAL RESTRAINING ORDERS IN DOMESTIC VIOLENCE CASES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Family Code section 6305, which limits when a family court may issue a mutual domestic violence restraining order -- one that restrains both Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan -- in the proceeding bearing case number CGC-26-123456 filed in Sacramento County. It states the text of section 6305, a related Penal Code provision it cross-references, and how one published California Court of Appeal decision has construed it. It does not state whether a mutual order should be requested, opposed, or is likely to be granted on the facts of this or any other case, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney.

SCOPE: A RESTRICTION ON MUTUAL ORDERS, NOT A GENERAL DVRO PROCEDURE
Section 6305 does not create a restraining order remedy of its own. It applies only where a court is considering restraining both parties to a domestic violence proceeding against each other in the same order -- a 'mutual order.' The general procedure for requesting a Domestic Violence Restraining Order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, including qualifying relationships, the statutory definition of abuse, the standard of proof, and firearm relinquishment, is addressed in this project's separate Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet and is not repeated here. This information sheet covers only the additional statutory conditions that apply specifically when a court is asked to, or is considering whether to, restrain both parties in a single mutual order.

STATUTORY CONDITION: PERSONAL APPEARANCE AND WRITTEN EVIDENCE FROM EACH PARTY
Family Code section 6305 states that a court shall not issue a mutual order enjoining the parties from specific acts of abuse described in section 6320 unless both of two conditions apply. The first condition is that both parties personally appear and each party presents written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in an application for relief using a mandatory Judicial Council restraining order application form. The statute specifies that written evidence of abuse or domestic violence contained in a responsive pleading does not, by itself, satisfy a party's obligation to present written evidence of abuse or domestic violence for this purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(a) The court shall not issue a mutual order enjoining the parties from specific acts of abuse described in Section 6320 unless both of the following apply:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(a) (California Legislative Information text), the introductory bar on mutual orders and the first of the two conditions that must both apply -- personal appearance and written evidence on a mandatory Judicial Council form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6305.)
  "(1) Both parties personally appear and each party presents written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in an application for relief using a mandatory Judicial Council restraining order application form. For purposes of this paragraph, written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in a responsive pleading does not satisfy the party’s obligation to present written evidence of abuse or domestic violence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the personal-appearance and written-evidence condition, and the statement that written evidence in a responsive pleading alone does not satisfy it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6305.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the personal-appearance and written-evidence condition in subdivision (a)(1); the separate detailed-findings condition in subdivision (a)(2) and the dominant-aggressor cross-reference in subdivision (b) are addressed in separate clauses. It does not cover the sentence in subdivision (a)(1) directing the Judicial Council to modify forms by July 1, 2016, which is spent and administrative. The leginfo.legislature.ca.gov source HTML renders the space after each subdivision letter/number (e.g., between "(a)" and "The court") as a non-breaking space ( , Unicode U+00A0) rather than an ordinary space; this was confirmed against the raw fetched HTML and is preserved verbatim, character-for-character, in the quotes below rather than being silently converted to a regular space. This clause does not address how a court applying section 6305 has treated evidence presented at a continued or later hearing, or what counts as an 'application for relief' beyond the mandatory Judicial Council form itself -- no case law on those points was reviewed for this clause.

STATUTORY CONDITION: DETAILED FINDINGS THAT BOTH PARTIES WERE PRIMARY AGGRESSORS
The second condition Family Code section 6305 requires before a mutual order may issue is that the court make detailed findings of fact indicating that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and that neither party acted primarily in self-defense. Both statutory conditions -- personal appearance with written evidence, and these detailed findings -- must be satisfied; the statute states that a mutual order shall not issue 'unless both of the following apply.'

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(2) The court makes detailed findings of fact indicating that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and that neither party acted primarily in self-defense."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the detailed-findings condition -- that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and neither acted primarily in self-defense (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6305.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only subdivision (a)(2). It does not state what quantum or type of evidence a court has found sufficient to support 'detailed findings' in a published decision, nor does it address subdivision (b)'s cross-reference to the Penal Code's dominant-aggressor factors, which is covered in a separate clause. The source HTML again renders the space after "(2)" as a non-breaking space, preserved verbatim in the quote below.

HOW 'PRIMARY AGGRESSOR' IS ASSESSED: THE PENAL CODE'S DOMINANT-AGGRESSOR FACTORS
Family Code section 6305(b) directs that, in determining whether both parties acted primarily as aggressors for purposes of the detailed-findings condition, the court shall consider the provisions concerning dominant aggressors set forth in Penal Code section 836(c)(3). That Penal Code provision, enacted for a different purpose -- identifying which party a peace officer may arrest when mutual protective orders are already in place -- states that the dominant aggressor is the person determined to be the most significant, rather than the first, aggressor, and lists four factors an officer is to consider in that identification: the intent of the law to protect victims of domestic violence from continuing abuse, the threats creating fear of physical injury, the history of domestic violence between the persons involved, and whether either person involved acted in self-defense.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(b) For purposes of subdivision (a), in determining if both parties acted
 primarily as aggressors, the court shall consider the provisions concerning dominant aggressors set forth in paragraph (3) of subdivision (c) of Section 836 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(b) (California Legislative Information text), the direction that, in determining whether both parties acted primarily as aggressors, the court shall consider the Penal Code's dominant-aggressor provisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6305.)
  "(3) In situations where mutual protective orders have been issued under Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code, liability for arrest under this subdivision applies only to those persons who are reasonably believed to have been the dominant aggressor."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 836(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of 'dominant aggressor' that Family Code section 6305(b) directs family courts to consider (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=836.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Family Code section 6305(b) in full and the arrest-context sentence identifying who qualifies as a 'dominant aggressor' under Penal Code section 836(c)(3); it does not quote the four lettered factors (A)-(D) that follow that sentence in the Penal Code, nor address how, if at all, a family court applying section 6305(b) has actually weighed those factors on a specific record -- no case law applying section 6305(b)'s cross-reference to a family-law fact pattern was located or reviewed for this clause. Penal Code section 836(c)(3) is written for peace officers deciding whom to arrest, not for family court judges deciding whether to issue a mutual order; section 6305(b) borrows its 'dominant aggressor' concept by cross-reference but does not restate it, so a reader comparing the two statutes should not assume every part of section 836(c)(3) transfers to the family-court context. The source HTML renders the space after "(b)" and after "(3)" as a non-breaking space (Unicode U+00A0) rather than an ordinary space, and wraps the sentence in section 6305(b) with a line break and leading whitespace between "acted" and "primarily"; both were confirmed against the raw fetched HTML and are preserved verbatim, character-for-character, in the quotes below rather than being silently converted to a regular space.

CASE LAW: A MUTUAL ORDER REQUIRES A REQUEST BY BOTH PARTIES
In a published 2015 decision, a California Court of Appeal addressed whether a trial court may issue a mutual restraining order under Family Code section 6305 when only one party has filed a written request for a restraining order and the responding party has not filed any request seeking restraints against the moving party. Construing section 6305 in the context of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act's statutory scheme, including the act's notice-of-hearing provisions, the court held that a mutual order may issue only where both parties have filed their own requests for that relief, so that each party receives the notice the statute otherwise contemplates.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "We conclude that a trial court may issue a mutual domestic violence restraining order under section 6305 only if both parties have filed requests for such relief, so as to give the requisite notice to the opposing party."
  — Isidora M. v. Silvino M. (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 11, 17-18 [190 Cal.Rptr.3d 502], holding that a trial court may issue a mutual DVRO under section 6305 only where both parties have filed their own requests for that relief (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2824899/isidora-m-v-silvino-m/)
  Known gap: This clause describes the holding of a single published Court of Appeal decision, Isidora M. v. Silvino M. (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 11; it is not a survey of all published decisions applying section 6305, and it does not address unpublished trial court rulings or how often courts issue mutual orders without a cross-request in practice. The court's reasoning rested substantially on legislative history and the statutory scheme surrounding section 6305 (including Family Code section 6302's notice requirement), which this clause summarizes but does not quote in full. CourtListener's opinion search was used (not raw retrieval from courtlistener.com, which this environment's network proxy blocks) and the exact holding sentence was verified as a literal, contiguous match in the opinion's full text via the search tool's document-search function (match_count: 1); the daily CourtListener search quota was not exhausted during this research.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing Family Code section 6305's two statutory conditions for a mutual domestic violence restraining order, its cross-reference to the Penal Code's dominant-aggressor factors, and the Isidora M. v. Silvino M. holding that a mutual order requires a request for that relief from each party. Signed in Oakland, California on September 7, 2026.
